title: Navajo voices on Bougainville
pull: A code the enemy never broke

facts.text: Navajo code talkers came ashore with the 3rd Marine Division at Bougainville on 1 November 1943. Pvt. Bill Toledo of the 3rd Battalion, 9th Marines, saw his first combat that day.
In this photo, Cpl. Henry Bake Jr. (left) and Pfc. George H. Kirk run a portable radio in a clearing they hacked out of dense jungle close behind the front lines on Bougainville, December 1943.
The first 29 Navajo recruits reported for Marine training in 1942 and built the code from their own language.
The code gave Navajo words to military terms. Aircraft took bird names, a submarine was besh lo, "iron fish," and the code word for America was "Our Mother."
Words not in the code were spelled out letter by letter, using a Navajo word whose English meaning began with that letter, such as wol la chee for A.
The code began with 211 terms, and talkers learned it by heart. Toledo memorized all 211.
Speed was the point. A colonel was won over when a Navajo team sent in two minutes a message that would have taken his own coders over an hour to encode and decode.
The night after the landing, a message stumped radiomen for three hours. Toledo was called in and, talking with another code talker at headquarters, decoded it in under five minutes.
Even Navajo speakers who were not trained code talkers could not understand the transmissions, because the code sat inside the language.
By war's end some 400 Navajos had served as code talkers.
The program stayed secret until it was declassified in 1968.
On 26 July 2001, President George W. Bush presented Congressional Gold Medals in the Capitol Rotunda honoring the original 29. Those who served later received silver medals.

photoNote: Cpl. Henry Bake Jr. and Pfc. George H. Kirk, Navajo code talkers, run a portable radio in a jungle clearing close behind the lines on Bougainville, December 1943. USMC photo 127-MN-69889-B (NARA 593415), public domain. From about a month after the 1 November landing; the card ties to the date because code talkers landed with the 3rd Marine Division. The negative number at the bottom was cropped off. NARA files the name as Bahe; the original caption reads Bake.
photoCredit: Navajo code talkers Cpl. Henry Bake Jr. and Pfc. George H. Kirk on Bougainville, December 1943. USMC photo, NARA 127-MN-69889-B, public domain.

declassified.fact: On Guadalcanal, a fellow Marine mistook code talker Bill Toledo for a Japanese soldier, took him prisoner at gunpoint, and wanted to shoot him until he was told Toledo was a Marine. That rifleman was then assigned to guard Toledo. Toledo did not learn the man had been his bodyguard until 40 years later.
